Third, informal adjudication is often conducted in the shadow of a 
trial-type, evidentiary hearing that will be available at a later stage of the 
adjudicative process if the agency and the affected party cannot come to 
agreement about the proper resolution of a matter. Recall that the purpose 
of a trial-type hearing is to conclusively resolve a dispute. Most adjudicative 
decisions are made during the initial, informal stage of the process and can 
be made final without any dispute from the affected party. In many cases, 
there is no basis for dispute because the agency is granting the party’s 
apphcation (e.g., for Social Security benefits or a license) or is dismissing a 
complaint against the party. In other cases, an agency may impose 
sanctions or take other adverse action based on undisputed (or not 
reasonably disputable) facts. For a discussion of how adjudication’s staged 
structure informed the APA, see Emily S. Bremer, The Rediscovered Stages 
of Agency Adjudication, 99 WASH. U. L. Re v . 377 (2021). This structure 
constrains agency discretion in the informal stage of the process by 
providing a powerful incentive for the agency to make a decision that is not 
(or cannot reasonably be) disputed. The practical reality that in most cases 
the affected party consents (or acquiesces) to the agency’s decision 
substantially reduces the number of cases that proceed to the hearing 
stage. The FAA example above reflects adjudication’s staged structure, as 
does the Social Security process described below in Richardson v. Perales, 
Although agencies that conduct adjudicative hearings typically do so 
because they are required to by statute, those hearings may or may not be 
subject to the APA’s minimum procedural requirements for formal 
hearings, to which we turn in the next section.
b. Trial-Type Evidentiary Hearings
The vast category of informal adjudication includes many trial-type, 
evidentiary hearings that are not conducted under the APA’s formal 
hearing provisions. Occasionafiy, such informal adjudicatory hearings are 
found where an agency has made a discretionary decision to conduct 
hearings in the absence of a statutory “hearing” requirement. (Recall that 
the APA’s hearing provisions apply only when a hearing is required by 
statute. See 5 U.S.C. § 554(a).) More often, however, informal adjudicatory 
hearings are found where an agency’s organic statute requires a “hearing” 
but does not require an “on-the-record” hearing. This may be because the 
matter falls within an exception to the APA’s hearing requirements (see 5 
U.S.C. § 554(a)(1)—(6)). Or because Congress has elected to deviate from 
the APA’s default procedures. Or because an agency has been able to avoid 
APA adjudication as the courts have adopted more deferential interpretive 
standards.
